mechanicsofinguinalcanal.exp: The inguinal canal is oblique, and its deep and superficial rings do not lie opposite one another, so raised intra-abdominal pressure does not act directly on the rings. Contraction of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis lowers the conjoint tendon like a shutter toward the inguinal ligament, narrowing the canal. The posterior wall is reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon, while the cremasteric and transversalis-fascia sling mechanisms help close the deep ring during straining.

riskfactorofdvt.exp: DVT risk follows Virchow's triad: venous stasis (immobility, bed rest, long travel, heart failure), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma, venous catheters), and hypercoagulability (malignancy, pregnancy or estrogen therapy, thrombophilia, prior VTE). Increasing age, obesity, smoking, and dehydration add risk.

primarysurveyoftraumatofemalehasmaxillof.exp: Use the trauma primary survey: A, secure the airway while protecting the cervical spine; with major maxillofacial trauma, suction blood and debris and prepare early for a definitive airway, including a surgical airway if necessary. B, assess and treat life-threatening breathing problems. C, control hemorrhage and restore circulation with large-bore IV access and blood products when indicated. D, assess neurologic status and glucose. E, fully expose the patient while preventing hypothermia, then reassess and arrange definitive care.

ddlateralneckswellings.exp: Differential diagnosis of a lateral neck swelling includes cervical lymphadenopathy (reactive, bacterial, tuberculous, lymphoma, or metastatic); branchial cleft cyst; cystic hygroma; carotid body or other neurogenic tumor; thyroid, parotid, or submandibular lesions; lipoma; dermoid/epidermoid cyst; and a deep neck abscess or laryngocele.

typesandddofdermoidcyst.exp: Dermoid-type cysts are classified histologically as epidermoid, true dermoid (with skin appendages), and teratoid cysts; they may be congenital inclusion cysts or acquired implantation cysts. The differential depends on site and includes an epidermal/sebaceous cyst, thyroglossal duct cyst, branchial cyst, ranula, cystic hygroma, lipoma, and an enlarged lymph node.

ddofinguinoscrotalswelling.exp: Differential diagnosis of an inguinoscrotal swelling includes an indirect inguinal hernia, communicating or funicular hydrocele, encysted cord hydrocele, varicocele, spermatocele/epididymal cyst, testicular tumor, epididymo-orchitis, testicular torsion, hematocele, undescended testis, and scrotal edema or a cord lipoma.

classificationsofhandinfection.exp: Hand infections are classified by site: superficial infections include paronychia, felon (pulp-space infection), and cellulitis; deep infections include pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, web-space (collar-button) abscess, thenar or mid-palmar space abscess, septic arthritis, and osteomyelitis. Bite wounds and infected wounds may involve more than one compartment.

riskfactorsofcancerbreast.exp: Important breast-cancer risk factors are female sex and increasing age; a personal history of breast cancer or high-risk lesions; family history and pathogenic BRCA1/BRCA2 or related variants; prior chest irradiation; prolonged estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity or late first birth); alcohol use; postmenopausal obesity; and combined menopausal hormone therapy. Risk is reduced by earlier first birth and breastfeeding.

complicationsofwoundhealing.exp: Complications of wound healing include infection, hematoma or seroma, delayed healing, wound dehiscence or incisional hernia, chronic sinus or fistula, hypertrophic scar or keloid, contracture, adhesions, and chronic ulceration. They may result from poor perfusion, infection, excessive tension, malnutrition, diabetes, smoking, or immunosuppression.

complicationsofherniaamscanner33924900.exp: Hernia complications include irreducibility (incarceration), intestinal obstruction, strangulation with ischemia or gangrene, inflammation of the sac or contents, and trauma or ulceration of the overlying skin. In inguinoscrotal hernia, pressure effects on the testis and recurrence after repair may also occur.

complicationsofhernia.exp: Hernia complications include irreducibility (incarceration), intestinal obstruction, strangulation with ischemia or gangrene, inflammation of the sac or contents, and trauma or ulceration of the overlying skin. In inguinoscrotal hernia, pressure effects on the testis and recurrence after repair may also occur.

whatarethegeneralprinciplesofsurgeryforh.exp: Principles are elevation and splintage of the hand, analgesia, removal of rings, assessment of neurovascular status, and prompt antibiotics when cellulitis or systemic infection is present. Obtain cultures when feasible. Drain any abscess promptly, debride necrotic tissue, remove a foreign body, and treat the involved space or tendon sheath; do not delay surgery for deep-space infection or flexor tenosynovitis. Check tetanus status and begin early hand therapy once acute infection is controlled.

comparebetweenbenignandmalignantlesions.exp: Benign lesions are usually slow-growing, well circumscribed or encapsulated, expansile rather than invasive, and do not metastasize; their cells are well differentiated and recurrence after complete excision is uncommon. Malignant lesions tend to grow rapidly, infiltrate and destroy adjacent tissues, show atypia and poor differentiation, may recur after excision, and can spread through lymphatics or blood. Exceptions occur, so histopathology is definitive.

enumeratecausesofsalivaryglandswellings.exp: Salivary-gland swellings may be inflammatory or infective (acute bacterial sialadenitis, viral mumps, chronic sialadenitis, Sjogren disease); obstructive (sialolithiasis or duct stenosis); neoplastic (benign pleomorphic adenoma/Warthin tumor or malignant salivary tumors); cystic (retention cyst or ranula); or systemic/non-neoplastic (HIV-associated disease, sarcoidosis, and sialadenosis associated with diabetes, alcohol use, or malnutrition). Regional lymph nodes and adjacent-organ lesions can mimic a gland swelling.

enumerategeneralandlocalcomplicationsofb.exp: Local complications include burn-wound infection, progressive tissue necrosis, edema, painful scarring, hypertrophic scars and contractures; circumferential burns may cause limb ischemia or restrict chest expansion, and facial or inhalational injury may obstruct the airway. General complications include burn shock and fluid/electrolyte loss, hypothermia, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure/ARDS, sepsis, stress ulceration, hypermetabolism and catabolism, and multiorgan failure.

a50yearoldfemalewithdiabetesmellitushadh.exp: This is an incisional hernia. Predisposing factors include wound infection or poor closure, obesity, diabetes, malnutrition, smoking, steroid or immunosuppressive therapy, increasing age, emergency surgery, and raised intra-abdominal pressure from cough, constipation, ascites, or urinary obstruction. Optimize weight, nutrition, glucose control, smoking, and cough/constipation before elective repair. Repair the defect, usually with mesh reinforcement, by an appropriate open or laparoscopic approach; urgent operation is required if obstruction or strangulation develops.

a30yearoldmalepresentswithtrismushegives.exp: Trismus several days after a contaminated foot wound is generalized tetanus until proved otherwise. Admit to intensive care with a low-stimulation environment, monitor and protect the airway, control spasms (usually benzodiazepines, with ventilation if needed), debride and clean the wound, and give human tetanus immune globulin (typically 500 IU IM for treatment) plus metronidazole. Start an active tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine at a separate site because tetanus does not confer immunity. Treat autonomic instability and provide nutrition and supportive care.

malechild10yearoldpresentedwithreddished.exp: Take the onset and duration of pain, trauma, fever, nausea/vomiting, urinary symptoms, prior episodes, and vaccination/sexual history; examine both testes for lie, tenderness, swelling, cremasteric reflex, inguinal hernia, and abdominal findings. Sudden severe pain, nausea/vomiting, a high or transverse testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex suggest torsion. Testicular torsion is the most dangerous cause: obtain immediate urologic assessment and urgent scrotal exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy; Doppler ultrasound may help if diagnosis is uncertain but must not delay surgery.

describediagnosisandtreatmentoffearlybre.exp: Diagnose by triple assessment: history and examination of both breasts and regional nodes, age-appropriate imaging (diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound, with MRI for selected indications), and image-guided core-needle biopsy for histology and ER/PR/HER2 testing. Stage the disease and discuss at a multidisciplinary team. For operable early disease, offer breast-conserving surgery with clear margins plus radiotherapy when suitable, or mastectomy when indicated; assess the axilla, usually with sentinel-node biopsy if clinically node-negative. Add endocrine, HER2-targeted, and/or chemotherapy according to stage, pathology, and biomarkers.

mentiondifferentialdiagnosisinvestigatio.exp: Differential diagnosis includes reactive or bacterial lymphadenitis, tuberculosis and other granulomatous infection, lymphoma, metastatic head-and-neck or thyroid cancer, and less often congenital cysts or salivary/thyroid lesions. Investigate with history and full head-and-neck examination, CBC and targeted infection tests, ultrasound, and needle sampling (FNAC or core biopsy); use CT/MRI and chest imaging when indicated, and excisional biopsy if lymphoma is suspected or needle sampling is nondiagnostic. For confirmed tuberculous lymphadenitis, treat with a full guideline-based multidrug anti-tuberculous regimen and monitor response.

comparebetweenarterialthrombosisandarter.exp: Arterial embolism is usually sudden, with abrupt severe ischemia in a previously asymptomatic limb; pulses may be normal in the other limb, and a source such as atrial fibrillation or recent myocardial infarction may be found. Thrombosis usually occurs in a limb with pre-existing atherosclerotic disease or chronic ischemic symptoms; pulses may be reduced in both limbs and collaterals may make onset less abrupt. Both require urgent limb-viability assessment, analgesia and immediate IV unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, followed by revascularization. Embolic occlusion is often treated by embolectomy; thrombosis may require thrombectomy, bypass, or endovascular treatment of the underlying lesion.

text_before.stem: As regard cancer; What are? (a) Definition (b) Etiology (c) Comparison between benign and malignant tumors (d) Diagnosis

asregardcancerwhataredefinitionetiologyd.exp: Cancer is a clonal malignant neoplasm caused by uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal cells, with invasion of surrounding tissue and potential metastasis. Etiology includes tobacco and alcohol, chemical carcinogens, ionizing or ultraviolet radiation, oncogenic infections, inherited cancer-predisposition mutations, chronic inflammation, and hormonal or lifestyle factors. Compared with benign tumors, malignant tumors are less circumscribed, invade adjacent tissue, may recur, show atypia and abnormal mitoses, and can metastasize. Diagnosis uses history and examination, appropriate imaging and endoscopy, and tissue confirmation by biopsy with histopathology; staging investigations are then selected according to the suspected primary site.

malepatient50yoldsmokerpresentedwithcerv.stem_fix: Male patient 50y old, smoker, presented with cervical lymph node swelling. How can you approach diagnosis? (4 marks)
malepatient50yoldsmokerpresentedwithcerv.text_note: Corrected joined words from the printed Q3 on source page 1.

text_before.stem: Male patient 50y old, smoker, presented withcervical lymph node swelling. How can you approach diagnosis?

malepatient50yoldsmokerpresentedwithcerv.exp: Take a history of duration and progression, pain, fever, weight loss, night sweats, tobacco and alcohol exposure, previous malignancy, and ear, nose, throat or respiratory symptoms. Examine all cervical nodes, the oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, thyroid, skin and other nodal areas, and look for a primary tumor. Investigate with blood tests as indicated, ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy, and imaging of the neck and chest; perform directed endoscopy or panendoscopy when an upper aerodigestive primary is suspected. If needle sampling is nondiagnostic, obtain an excisional biopsy and arrange staging based on histology.

obesediabeticfemalepatient50yoldpisthist.stem_fix: Obese, diabetic female patient 50y old, past history of right modified mastectomy, presented with right upper limb edema (4 marks): (a) Enumerate expected causes? (b) Mention approach to diagnosis?

obesediabeticfemalepatient50yoldpisthist.exp: Expected causes include post-mastectomy lymphatic disruption or radiotherapy causing lymphedema, recurrent tumor or axillary nodal disease obstructing lymphatics or veins, upper-limb deep venous thrombosis, cellulitis, and less commonly trauma or systemic fluid-retaining disease. Assess onset, progression, pain, fever, venous catheter history and cancer treatment; compare both arms and examine the skin, pulses, veins, axilla and chest wall for infection or recurrence. Measure arm circumference, request duplex ultrasound if thrombosis is possible, and investigate suspected recurrence with breast or axillary imaging and biopsy of a suspicious lesion. Use blood tests and cardiac, renal or hepatic assessment when systemic edema is suspected.

asregardbreastabscessmentiondiagnosisdif.exp: Breast abscess is diagnosed from a painful, tender, fluctuant breast mass, often with erythema and fever; use ultrasound to confirm a collection and guide aspiration, and culture aspirated pus. Differential diagnoses include mastitis without abscess, an infected cyst, galactocele, and inflammatory breast carcinoma, especially when findings persist or are atypical. Treat with analgesia, continued breast emptying or feeding when appropriate, and antibiotics covering likely staphylococci; drain the collection by ultrasound-guided needle aspiration or incision and drainage when large, loculated, or not resolving, and reassess to exclude an underlying malignancy.

malepatient25yoldpresentedtoemergencyroo.exp: Treat hemorrhagic shock from blood loss: control bleeding, give oxygen, establish large-bore IV access, send blood for grouping and crossmatch, and resuscitate with warmed blood products as indicated. Before transfusion, confirm patient identity and compatibility, check the unit and expiry, use a suitable filter and line, record baseline observations, begin slowly, and monitor for reactions. Other possible shock types include septic shock if the wound becomes infected and neurogenic shock if there is associated injury. Tetanus may cause trismus, risus sardonicus, neck and abdominal rigidity, painful stimulus-induced generalized spasms, opisthotonus, dysphagia, and autonomic instability.

malepatient40yoldpresentedwithsulphorica.exp: Protect rescuers, remove contaminated clothing and jewelry, brush away dry chemical, then irrigate the skin and eyes copiously with clean running water; do not attempt chemical neutralization. Assess airway, breathing and circulation, provide analgesia, cover the irrigated burn with a clean dry sheet, and arrange urgent burn care. Other reasons for hospital admission include a large or deep burn; burns involving the eyes, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum or major joints; suspected inhalation injury; electrical or chemical burns; circumferential burns; associated trauma or significant comorbidity; uncontrolled pain; or inadequate home support.

whatarethecausesandmainclinicalsymptomso.exp: Chronic limb ischemia is caused mainly by atherosclerotic occlusive disease; less common causes include thromboangiitis obliterans, embolic disease, vasculitis, and aneurysmal disease. Risk factors include smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and older age. Symptoms progress from intermittent claudication to rest pain, often worse at night and relieved by dependency, then ischemic ulceration or gangrene. Examination may show cool pale skin, delayed capillary refill, reduced or absent pulses, dependent rubor, shiny skin, hair loss, and tissue loss.

whataretheriskfactorsforimpairedwoundhea.exp: Risk factors for impaired wound healing include poor perfusion or ischemia, infection, foreign material, devitalized tissue, excessive tension or repeated trauma, edema, and poor wound apposition. Systemic factors include malnutrition, diabetes, smoking, anemia, hypoxia, renal or hepatic disease, malignancy, advanced age, obesity, and immunosuppression. Corticosteroids and cytotoxic drugs can also impair healing.

defineshockanddescribemanagementofhypovo.exp: Shock is acute circulatory failure causing inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery, with cellular dysfunction and potential organ failure. Hypovolemic shock is managed by immediate assessment and resuscitation: secure the airway and give oxygen, control external or internal bleeding, obtain two large-bore IV lines, send blood for crossmatch and investigations, and rapidly restore circulating volume with warmed blood products when hemorrhage is present (or isotonic crystalloid while blood is arranged when appropriate). Monitor mental status, pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, urine output, lactate, and response to treatment; identify and treat the source, prevent hypothermia, and escalate to surgery or interventional control of bleeding when indicated.

differentialdiagnosisofbasalcellcarcinom.exp: Differential diagnoses of basal cell carcinoma include squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma, seborrheic keratosis, actinic keratosis, benign melanocytic nevus, amelanotic melanoma, dermatofibroma, and chronic ulcer or scar. Diagnosis is confirmed by an appropriately planned skin biopsy when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain or treatment planning requires histology.

a50yearoldfemalepresentswithdiffuseredne.exp: The likely diagnosis is acute cellulitis of the right leg, with possible abscess or deeper infection to exclude. Common organisms are beta-hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA where relevant. Assess vital signs, sepsis, extent, skin breaks, pulses, sensation, and glucose; look for fluctuance, crepitus, pain out of proportion, or systemic toxicity. Mark the erythema, elevate the limb, provide analgesia and fluids as needed, optimize diabetes control, and start antibiotics covering streptococci and staphylococci according to severity and local guidance; obtain cultures in severe or purulent disease. Drain any abscess, admit for systemic illness or rapid progression, and urgently explore suspected necrotizing infection.

whataredifferentialdiagnosesoflateralnec.exp: Differential diagnoses of a lateral neck swelling include reactive or metastatic lymphadenopathy, lymphoma, branchial cleft cyst, cystic hygroma, carotid body tumor, parotid-tail lesion, lipoma, and a thyroid or salivary lesion. In an adult, a persistent unexplained mass must be assessed for malignancy. For a branchial cleft cyst, take a history and examine the oral cavity, pharynx, thyroid, and neck; use neck ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration, with CT or MRI when needed to define anatomy and exclude a primary malignancy. Treat any acute infection first, then excise the cyst and tract completely after diagnostic assessment.

enumerateriskfactorsforcancerbreast.exp: Breast cancer risk factors include increasing age, female sex, personal history of breast cancer or high-risk lesions, pathogenic BRCA1/BRCA2 or other hereditary mutations, strong family history, prolonged estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, or first full-term pregnancy at older age), postmenopausal obesity, alcohol use, prior chest irradiation, and dense breast tissue. Hormone replacement therapy can also increase risk, particularly combined therapy with longer use.

whataredifferentialdiagnosisofpainfulscr.exp: Differential diagnoses of painful scrotal swelling include testicular torsion, epididymo-orchitis, torsion of a testicular appendage, incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia, trauma, and less commonly tumor with hemorrhage. Testicular torsion typically causes sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea or vomiting, a high-riding transverse testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex; fever and urinary symptoms are usually absent. Perform urgent examination and urinalysis; Doppler ultrasound may help only if it does not delay treatment. Suspected torsion requires immediate scrotal exploration, detorsion, and bilateral orchiopexy; orchiectomy is required if the testis is nonviable.

22yearsoldfemaleaccidentallydiscoveredpa.exp: The most likely diagnosis is a fibroadenoma, but malignancy must be excluded by triple assessment: history and examination, age-appropriate imaging (ultrasound is usually first-line at age 22), and image-guided core biopsy if imaging or clinical findings are suspicious or the lesion is enlarging. Differential diagnoses include a breast cyst, phyllodes tumor, fibrocystic change, and (rarely at this age) breast carcinoma. If imaging and examination are concordant and benign, explain the diagnosis and observe with follow-up; excise if the mass is large, growing, symptomatic, atypical, or the patient prefers removal.

50yearsoldmalecomplainingfromintermitten.exp: The most likely diagnosis is an irreducible obstructed inguinoscrotal hernia with suspected strangulation, given the recent irreducibility, vomiting, and new pain. Differential diagnoses include a hydrocele, testicular or epididymal mass, varicocele, and an acute scrotal condition; an incarcerated femoral hernia is another possible cause of bowel obstruction. Complications include intestinal obstruction, strangulation with bowel ischemia or gangrene, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and testicular ischemia. Resuscitate urgently: assess airway, breathing, and circulation; keep the patient nil by mouth; give oxygen as indicated; establish two large-bore IV lines; send blood count, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, and group and cross-match; give warmed IV fluids, analgesia, and nasogastric decompression for vomiting or obstruction; monitor vital signs and urine output with a catheter. Give perioperative broad-spectrum antibiotics and obtain urgent surgical review. Do not delay operation for imaging when strangulation is suspected. Perform emergency exploration, reduce the hernia, assess bowel viability, resect nonviable bowel with appropriate anastomosis, and repair the hernia; avoid mesh if the operative field is contaminated or infected.

factorsaffectingwoundhealing.exp: Factors affecting wound healing include general and local factors. General factors are older age, malnutrition (including deficiencies of vitamins A and C, protein, or zinc), chronic disease such as diabetes or cancer, corticosteroid therapy, and irradiation. Local factors include reduced vascularity, excessive wound tension, immobilization, foreign bodies or necrotic tissue, infection, and poor tissue apposition or adherence to an underlying bony surface.

summarizetttofhypovolemicshock.exp: Treat hypovolemic shock with immediate ABC resuscitation: secure the airway, support breathing and give oxygen, and control external bleeding while restoring circulation. Establish large-bore IV access, send blood for investigations and cross-match, and give warmed isotonic crystalloid while arranging early blood products for ongoing major hemorrhage. Identify and control the cause, including urgent exploration and repair of bleeding when indicated; immobilize associated fractures and keep the patient warm. Monitor pulse, blood pressure, temperature, mental state, urine output, blood gases and, when indicated, central venous pressure. Avoid fluid overload and use inotropes only when appropriate after adequate volume resuscitation.

generalcomplicationsofburn.exp: Major burns can cause hypovolemic shock and multisystem complications. Respiratory complications include inhalational injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome; renal complications include acute kidney injury; gastrointestinal complications include stress ulceration and paralytic ileus. Cardiovascular depression may reduce cardiac output. Extensive burns can cause anemia and hypoproteinemia, while the endocrine stress response increases catecholamines, cortisol and antidiuretic hormone. Infection and sepsis are important later complications.

complicationsofbloodtransfusion.exp: Transfusion complications may affect the donor or recipient. Donor complications include vasovagal or neurogenic symptoms, anemia after excessive donation, and local thrombophlebitis. Immediate recipient complications include circulatory overload, acute hemolytic reaction, febrile or pyrogenic reaction, allergic reaction, thrombophlebitis and air embolism. Massive transfusion may cause hypothermia, arrhythmias, citrate-related hypocalcemia, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, hyperkalemia, pulmonary microembolism and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. Delayed complications include transfusion-transmitted infections such as hepatitis B or C, HIV, syphilis, brucellosis and malaria.

comparebetweensubcutaneouslipomaandsebac.exp: A subcutaneous lipoma is a benign adipose tumor, usually a soft, lobulated, mobile, painless mass with a slippery edge; it may be attached to the skin at multiple points and is generally superficial to muscle. Treatment is observation or enucleation/excision when symptomatic, enlarging or diagnostically uncertain. A sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst is a small, well-defined cystic swelling attached to the skin at a punctum, often containing keratin. It may become infected and suppurate. Definitive treatment is complete excision of the cyst wall when inflammation has settled; drain an acute abscess if present.

comparebetweenacutelactitionalmastitisma.exp: Acute lactational mastitis has an acute onset and rapidly progressive course, usually with high fever, fiery red overlying skin, marked tenderness and firm tender axillary nodes. It generally improves with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care. Mastitis carcinomatosa has a gradual onset and slowly progressive course, often with low-grade fever, dusky red skin, mild tenderness and hard, non-tender axillary nodes. It does not respond to antibiotics and requires urgent assessment and treatment as inflammatory breast cancer.

ddofmidlineneckswellings.exp: Differential diagnoses of a midline neck swelling include solid and cystic lesions. Solid causes include an enlarged submental or pretracheal/prelaryngeal lymph node and a thyroid isthmus nodule. Cystic causes include a thyroglossal duct cyst, dermoid cyst, cold abscess, subhyoid bursitis, laryngocele and a cystic lesion of the thyroid isthmus. A thyroglossal duct cyst typically moves with swallowing and protrusion of the tongue; examination and targeted neck imaging help distinguish the causes.

ddofacutescrotalswellings.exp: Differential diagnoses of acute scrotal swelling include testicular torsion, acute epididymo-orchitis, hematocele, pyocele, acute funiculitis and a strangulated oblique inguinal hernia. Testicular torsion is a time-critical diagnosis and must be excluded urgently; sudden severe pain, a high-riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex support it. Clinical examination and Doppler ultrasonography can help when they do not delay necessary exploration.

ddoftongueulcers.exp: Differential diagnoses of tongue ulcers include traumatic, inflammatory, infectious, premalignant and malignant lesions. Traumatic causes include a frenular ulcer after local trauma and an ulcer from a sharp tooth. Inflammatory or infectious causes include aphthous or dyspeptic ulcers, multiple small herpetic ulcers, oral lichen planus, tuberculosis, syphilis and chronic superficial glossitis. Premalignant lesions include leukoplakia and erythroplakia; benign lesions include papilloma. A persistent ulcer, especially on the lateral tongue, an indurated or raised ulcer, or an ulcer with cervical nodes requires biopsy to exclude squamous cell carcinoma.

cpofdvt.exp: Deep vein thrombosis may be asymptomatic or present with unilateral leg pain, swelling and tenderness. Examination may show warmth, erythema, pitting edema and dilated superficial veins. Compare both limbs and assess for risk factors and signs of pulmonary embolism. Homan sign is unreliable and should not be used to exclude DVT; confirm suspected disease with a validated clinical assessment and venous duplex ultrasonography.

hardsignsofvascularinjury.exp: Hard signs of arterial injury include active or pulsatile external bleeding, an expanding or pulsatile hematoma, a palpable thrill or bruit, and distal ischemia with absent pulses. Ischemic findings include pallor, pain, progressive coldness, paresthesia and paralysis. These findings warrant urgent vascular assessment and operative control or repair as indicated.

importanceofpreoperativelaboratoryinvest.exp: Preoperative laboratory investigations help identify medical conditions that require treatment before surgery and reduce avoidable perioperative morbidity and mortality. They provide a baseline and help assess anemia, bleeding risk, renal or metabolic problems and other relevant comorbidity. The findings also help the team anticipate anesthesia-specific risks such as airway problems, malignant hyperthermia, nausea and vomiting, or postoperative delirium. The preoperative assessment should explain material risks to the patient and support informed consent.

boundariesofhasselbachtriangle.exp: The boundaries of Hesselbach triangle are the lateral border of rectus abdominis medially, the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, and the inguinal ligament inferiorly. The triangle is the site of direct inguinal hernias.

contentsoffemoralsheath.exp: The femoral sheath is formed anteriorly by transversalis fascia and posteriorly by iliac fascia. It contains three compartments: the lateral compartment contains the femoral artery, the intermediate compartment contains the femoral vein, and the medial compartment is the femoral canal, which contains loose connective tissue, lymphatics and the deep inguinal node of Cloquet. The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath, lateral to it.

malepatient1syearsoldpresentedwithlatera.exp:
A. Types of shock: initially hypovolemic (hemorrhagic) shock from blood loss due to the grade II liver laceration with intraperitoneal collection (hypotension 90/60, tachycardia 130, tachypnea, hemoglobin 7 g/l); now, 4 days later, with fever 38.5C and leukocytosis 18000, septic shock is superimposed (infected intraperitoneal collection / peritonitis), so it is a mixed hypovolemic and septic shock.
B. SIRS: systemic inflammatory response to any insult (infective or not) with two or more of: temperature above 38C or below 36C, heart rate above 90/min, respiratory rate above 20/min or PaCO2 below 32 mmHg, WBC above 12000 or below 4000/mm3 or more than 10% immature bands. Sepsis: SIRS with a documented or suspected source of infection (now defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, SOFA increase of 2 or more). Septic shock: sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to keep mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg or more and serum lactate above 2 mmol/l despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
C. Management: ABC resuscitation (ATLS), oxygen, two large-bore IV cannulae, blood sampling for grouping and cross-matching, CBC, coagulation, renal and liver functions, lactate and blood cultures; fluid resuscitation with crystalloids and blood transfusion to correct hemoglobin; urinary catheter and CVP monitoring of output; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics started early; drainage of the infected intraperitoneal collection (CT/US-guided percutaneous drainage or laparotomy/laparoscopy with peritoneal lavage), and control of liver bleeding (conservative management for stable grade II injury, angioembolization, or operative hemostasis if unstable); vasopressors (noradrenaline) if hypotension persists after fluids; ICU care, correction of acidosis and electrolytes, nutritional support, DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis.

yarldmalepresentstotheoutpatientclinicco.exp:
A. Most likely diagnosis: chronic lower limb ischemia (critical limb ischemia) of the right lower limb due to Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), presenting with intermittent claudication progressing to rest pain and ischemic ulceration.
B. Supporting factors: young male (34 years); heavy smoker (20 cigarettes/day for 15 years); no diabetes or hypertension (atherosclerosis less likely); distal (infrapopliteal) disease with weak dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses; progression from claudication (claudication distance 50 meters) to rest pain at night and a painful ulcer on the tip of the big toe with a pale foot.
C. Investigations: ankle brachial pressure index; arterial duplex ultrasound; CT angiography or conventional angiography (segmental occlusion of small and medium distal arteries with corkscrew collaterals and normal proximal arteries); investigations to exclude other causes: blood sugar, lipid profile, autoimmune and coagulation screens, echocardiography to exclude embolic source.
D. Principles of management: complete and permanent cessation of smoking (the most important measure); foot care, treatment of the ulcer and infection, analgesia; supervised exercise; drugs: antiplatelets, vasodilators such as prostacyclin analogues (iloprost), cilostazol; lumbar sympathectomy for rest pain and superficial ulcers; revascularization (bypass) rarely possible because of distal disease; conservative amputation of the gangrenous toe when needed, and major amputation for extensive gangrene.

45yearsoldfemalepresentedwithbreastmassa.exp:
A. Risk factors for breast cancer: female sex and increasing age; family history in first-degree relatives (as her mother) and BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations; previous breast cancer or atypical hyperplasia (ductal/lobular) and LCIS; prolonged estrogen exposure: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, first full-term pregnancy after 30 years, no breast feeding, hormone replacement therapy and oral contraceptives; obesity after menopause, alcohol intake, high-fat diet; previous chest wall irradiation; high socioeconomic class and Western lifestyle.
B. Signs of breast cancer: hard, irregular, painless lump, commonly in the upper outer quadrant, with ill-defined edge; fixation to skin (skin dimpling, peau d'orange, ulceration, satellite nodules) or to deep structures (pectoral fascia, chest wall); nipple retraction or deviation, bloody nipple discharge, eczematous nipple changes (Paget's disease); axillary lymph nodes that are hard, discrete, later matted or fixed, and supraclavicular nodes; arm lymphedema; signs of distant metastases (bone pain and pathological fractures, hepatomegaly and jaundice, pleural effusion, neurological deficits); cachexia.
C. Benign versus malignant neoplasms: benign tumors grow slowly, are well differentiated, encapsulated and well defined, grow by expansion, do not invade or metastasize, rarely recur after excision and have little systemic effect (except pressure or hormone secretion); malignant tumors grow rapidly, range from well to poorly differentiated (anaplasia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, abnormal mitoses), are non-encapsulated with ill-defined edges, infiltrate and destroy surrounding tissues, spread by lymphatics, blood and implantation (metastasis), commonly recur after excision, and cause systemic effects (cachexia, anemia, paraneoplastic syndromes) and may be fatal.

60yearsoldmalepresentedwithirreduciblein.exp:
A. Most probable diagnosis: strangulated (obstructed) recurrent right inguinal hernia (irreducible, with intestinal obstruction features: vomiting and absolute constipation; red, tender, hot swelling with fever and tachycardia).
B. Risk factors for wound failure (and hernia recurrence): patient factors: old age, obesity, malnutrition and hypoproteinemia, anemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, jaundice, uremia, malignancy, steroid or cytotoxic therapy, chronic cough, constipation or urinary straining raising intra-abdominal pressure; local and technical factors: wound infection, hematoma or seroma, poor blood supply, tension on the repair, improper suture material or technique, poor tissue quality, and early strenuous activity.
C. Management: urgent admission, nil by mouth, nasogastric tube suction, IV fluids and correction of electrolytes, IV antibiotics, analgesia, urinary catheter; no attempt at forcible reduction (taxis); emergency surgical exploration: open the sac and inspect the contents; if bowel is viable, reduce it; if gangrenous, resect with anastomosis; ligate the sac and repair the defect (tissue repair such as herniorrhaphy in a contaminated field, or mesh hernioplasty when the field is clean); postoperative care and treatment of predisposing factors.
D. Differential diagnosis of scrotal swellings: inguinoscrotal hernia; hydrocele (vaginal, congenital, infantile, encysted hydrocele of the cord); hematocele; varicocele; epididymal cyst and spermatocele; acute epididymo-orchitis and chronic (tuberculous) epididymitis; torsion of the testis; testicular tumor; gumma of the testis; scrotal skin lesions (sebaceous cysts, carcinoma of the scrotum, Fournier's gangrene); lipoma of the cord.

malepatient15yearsoldpresentedwithlatera.exp:
A. Most probable diagnosis: lymphoma, most likely Hodgkin's lymphoma (young patient, lateral neck lymphadenopathy with B symptoms - fever, weight loss - and splenomegaly, not responding to antibiotics).
B. Boundaries of neck triangles: anterior triangle: anteriorly the midline of the neck, posteriorly the anterior border of sternomastoid, superiorly (base) the lower border of the mandible; it is subdivided into submental, submandibular (digastric), carotid and muscular triangles. Posterior triangle: anteriorly the posterior border of sternomastoid, posteriorly the anterior border of trapezius, inferiorly (base) the middle third of the clavicle, apex at the meeting of sternomastoid and trapezius at the superior nuchal line; roof is the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, floor is the prevertebral fascia over the muscles (splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenes); the inferior belly of omohyoid divides it into occipital and supraclavicular (subclavian) triangles.
C. Investigations: CBC with differential, ESR, LDH, liver and renal functions; neck ultrasound; excisional lymph node biopsy for histopathology and immunohistochemistry (Reed-Sternberg cells, CD15/CD30) - FNAC is not sufficient; tuberculin test and chest X-ray to exclude tuberculosis; staging by CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET-CT; bone marrow biopsy when indicated; abdominal ultrasound for splenomegaly.
D. Differential diagnosis: lymph node causes: tuberculous lymphadenitis, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, infectious mononucleosis and other viral infections, toxoplasmosis, leukemia, sarcoidosis, secondary deposits, HIV; non-nodal lateral neck swellings: branchial cyst, cystic hygroma, carotid body tumor, neurofibroma, lipoma, sternomastoid tumor, cold abscess.

regardingcircumferentialburnmentionthefo.exp:
A. Definition: a full-thickness (deep) burn involving the whole circumference of a limb, the chest, the neck or a digit, producing a rigid inelastic eschar that acts as a tourniquet as edema accumulates under it.
B. Complications: limbs - progressive venous then arterial obstruction with compartment syndrome, distal ischemia, nerve and muscle necrosis, gangrene and loss of the limb, rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury; chest - restriction of chest wall movement with hypoventilation, respiratory failure and hypoxia; neck - compression of the airway and venous return; later - infection and sepsis, and circumferential contracture with deformity and hypertrophic scarring.
C. Treatment: general burn resuscitation (ABC, fluid resuscitation by Parkland formula, analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, monitoring of urine output); elevation of the limb and monitoring of distal circulation (pulses, capillary refill, Doppler, compartment pressure) and ventilation; urgent escharotomy - longitudinal incisions through the full thickness of the eschar along the midlateral and midmedial lines of the limb (and digits), or along the anterior axillary lines with a transverse subcostal incision for the chest, until the tissues bulge and circulation or ventilation improves; fasciotomy if compartment syndrome persists; followed by excision of dead tissue and skin grafting, physiotherapy and splinting to prevent contractures.

whatistrueofcystichygromaitarisesfromswe.exp: Cystic hygroma is a congenital macrocystic lymphatic malformation that arises from sequestered lymphatic sacs. It is characteristically soft, compressible, painless, and displays brilliant translucence on transillumination.

thesurfaceareaoftheperitonealmembraneisn.exp: True. The surface area of the peritoneal membrane in an adult is approximately 1.7 to 2.0 square meters, which is roughly equivalent to the total cutaneous surface area.

theparietalperitoneumispoorlyinnervated.exp: False. The parietal peritoneum is richly innervated by somatic afferent nerves (intercostal and subcostal nerves, phrenic nerve) and is exquisitely sensitive to sharp, localized pain, pressure, and temperature.

theperitoneumhasthecapacitytoabsorblarge.exp: True. The peritoneum has a remarkable absorptive capacity (absorbing up to several liters of fluid per day), primarily via lymphatic stomata located on the peritoneal surface of the diaphragm.

theperitoneumhastheabilitytoproducefibri.exp: True. Normal peritoneal mesothelial cells produce tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), providing intrinsic fibrinolytic activity to prevent permanent fibrous adhesion formation; this activity decreases during inflammation and ischemia.

thepainneverradiatestothebackandthisdiff.exp: False. In acute pancreatitis or peptic ulcer perforation, pain frequently radiates straight through to the back (at T10-L2 levels), whereas biliary colic pain typically radiates to the right infrascapular area.

vomitingisanotablefeature.exp: True. Vomiting is a prominent early clinical sign in high small bowel mechanical obstruction and acute peritonitis, often following the onset of severe abdominal pain.

bleedingisrare.exp: True. In simple uncomplicated mechanical bowel obstruction, intraluminal bleeding is rare unless vascular strangulation, mucosal infarction, or an underlying ulcerated malignancy is present.

theymaycausegastricoutletobstructiont.exp: True. Chronic peptic ulcer disease in the pyloric channel or duodenal bulb, as well as prepyloric gastric adenocarcinoma, are major causes of gastric outlet obstruction due to cicatricial stenosis or mechanical blockage.

weightlossisatypicalsymptom.exp: True. Significant unintentional weight loss is a hallmark symptom of malignant gastrointestinal tumors, chronic mesenteric ischemia, and advanced gastric outlet obstruction.

pancreaticinjuryiscommonfollowingbluntab.exp: False. The retroperitoneal location of the pancreas protects it, making traumatic injury relatively uncommon (occurring in fewer than 5-10% of blunt abdominal trauma cases), typically resulting from severe compressive force against the vertebral column.

pancreaticinjuryisoftenaccompaniedbydama.exp: True. Because high force is required to injure the retroperitoneal pancreas, associated injuries to contiguous organs (liver, spleen, duodenum, and major abdominal vessels) occur in over 70% of cases.

theserumamylaseisraisedinmostcasesofpanc.exp: True. Serum amylase and lipase levels are elevated in approximately 70-80% of patients with significant pancreatic parenchyma or ductal trauma, although initial normal levels do not rule out injury.

itismostcommoninchildrenwithapeakinciden.exp: True. Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception has its peak clinical incidence between 5 and 10 months of age, coinciding with the introduction of solid foods and adenovirus-associated lymphoid hyperplasia.

about10percentofinfantileintussusception.exp: False. Over 90% of intussusceptions occurring in infants and young children under 2 years of age are idiopathic (due to hypertrophied Peyer patches), with identifiable anatomical lead points found in only about 5-10%.

itcausesobstructionbutnotstrangulation.exp: False. Intussusception causes progressive mechanical obstruction and, if untreated, leads to venous congestion, ischemia, bowel wall necrosis, strangulation, perforation, and peritonitis.

meckelsdiverticulumcanbeacauseinolderchi.exp: True. In children older than 2 years and adults, intussusception is most commonly caused by an identifiable pathological lead point, of which Meckel's diverticulum and polyps are the most frequent.
